questions.stem: What is the difference between a base and an alkali?

options.text: An alkali is stronger than a base
There is no difference; they are the same thing
A base dissolves in water; an alkali does not
A base is any substance that neutralises an acid; an alkali is a base that dissolves in water

questions.explanation: A base is any substance that can neutralise an acid. An alkali is a specific type of base that is soluble in water, producing OH⁻ ions in solution.

questions.stem: What ion do alkalis produce when dissolved in water?
questions.explanation: Alkalis produce OH⁻ (hydroxide) ions when dissolved in water. It is these hydroxide ions that give alkaline solutions their characteristic properties.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a base but NOT an alkali?
questions.explanation: Copper oxide is a base because it can neutralise acids, but it is not an alkali because it does not dissolve in water. Sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are both soluble bases (alkalis).

questions.stem: What is the pH range of alkaline solutions?
questions.explanation: Alkaline solutions have a pH greater than 7. The higher the pH, the more alkaline the solution. A pH of 14 represents a very strong alkali.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a common alkali used in the laboratory?
questions.explanation: Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) is a common laboratory alkali. It is soluble in water and produces a strongly alkaline solution with a high pH.

questions.stem: What colour does red litmus paper turn in an alkaline solution?
questions.explanation: Alkalis turn red litmus paper blue. This is the opposite of acids, which turn blue litmus paper red.

questions.stem: Which everyday substance is an example of an alkali?
questions.explanation: Oven cleaner contains sodium hydroxide, which is a strong alkali. Lemon juice, vinegar, and fizzy drinks are all acidic.
